titel: Choosing an ETF in the US
kurz: Why the name does not matter when choosing among thousands of US-listed products, and in which order you check the index, the fund structure and the costs.

bloecke.md:
US exchanges list several thousand exchange-traded products, and not all of them are funds. An ETF in the narrow sense is an investment company registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940. Its assets are held by a custodian, separately from the assets of the fund manager. An exchange-traded note (ETN) is an unsecured debt security and carries the default risk of the issuing bank. Many commodity products are structured as grantor trusts or commodity pools, with tax rules of their own. An investor who buys a gold product because the search screen shows it next to the stock ETFs has thereby already made the first selection decision without noticing.

The selection itself consists of two decisions of very different weight. The first concerns the index, that is, the markets, countries and company sizes in which the fund invests. It determines almost the entire return. The second concerns the wrapper, that is, the question of which provider tracks this index in which legal form and at what ongoing costs. For broad index ETFs at today's US expense ratios, it accounts for hundredths to tenths of a percentage point. In practice, the second decision usually receives more attention than the first.

bloecke.unter: At the top are the criteria that determine the return, at the bottom those that shift it only by fractions. Public discussion usually starts with the lower ones.

bloecke.md:
## Choosing the index (step 1)

For US investors, the first question is whether to hold only the US market or the whole world. The S&P 500 contains around 500 large US companies and, according to S&P Dow Jones Indices, covers about 80% of the available US market capitalization. Total market indices such as the CRSP US Total Market Index, the S&P Total Market Index or the Dow Jones U.S. Broad Stock Market Index add mid and small caps and contain several thousand stocks. Because the largest companies dominate both, the returns of the S&P 500 and of the total market have been close over long periods, but they are not the same.

The world indices are not interchangeable either. The MSCI ACWI covers developed and emerging markets in 47 countries with around 2,410 large and mid-sized stocks (as of August 2026). The FTSE Global All Cap Index adds small caps and contains several thousand stocks. FTSE classifies South Korea as a developed market, MSCI as an emerging market. A US-only portfolio ties the entire stock allocation to one economy and one currency. A world portfolio holds roughly 60% to 70% in US stocks anyway, depending on the index.

bloecke.md: All of these funds are domiciled in the US. The expense ratios of broad core ETFs from the large providers are typically between 0.03% and 0.10% a year; check the current figure in the prospectus, because providers cut them regularly. Several of these ETFs are a share class of a larger fund. At Vanguard, for example, many ETFs are a share class of the index mutual fund with the same name, so the fund as a whole is much larger than the ETF class alone. Whether a product is large enough is measured by the fund as a whole rather than by the individual class. Each size figure also comes with a reference date.

## Fund structure and costs beyond the expense ratio (step 2)

The expense ratio states the published ongoing costs. The [[Tracking difference|tracking difference]], by contrast, measures how far the fund return lagged behind the index return. It also includes transaction costs, sampling deviations, withholding tax effects and income from securities lending. Comparing two ETFs on the expense ratio alone can therefore lead to the wrong result.

For US investors, the question of domicile has a simple answer: buy funds domiciled in the US. A US fund holding US stocks pays no withholding tax on their dividends. For international stock funds, foreign countries withhold tax on the dividends at fund level. A US fund with more than half of its assets in foreign stocks can pass this tax through to you, and you can claim it as a foreign tax credit (26 U.S.C. § 853). In an IRA or 401(k), the credit is lost, which is one reason to hold international funds in a taxable account.

The second question is the legal structure, and the ticker says nothing about it. A 1940 Act ETF passes qualified dividends and long-term gains through at the normal rates. Physical gold and silver trusts are taxed as collectibles, with a maximum rate of 28% on long-term gains instead of 20% (26 U.S.C. § 1(h)(4)). Commodity funds organized as partnerships send a Schedule K-1 instead of a Form 1099. ETNs carry the credit risk of the issuer. The prospectus states the structure on its first pages.

bloecke.titel: Foreign funds: 15% or up to 37% plus interest
bloecke.md: ETFs domiciled outside the US, such as the Irish and Luxembourg UCITS ETFs popular in Europe (ISINs beginning with IE or LU), are passive foreign investment companies (PFICs) for US persons. Without a special election, a gain of $10,000 after several years is taxed largely at the highest ordinary rate of 37%, which gives around $3,700 plus an interest charge, instead of $1,500 at the 15% long-term rate. On top of this comes Form 8621 every year. The elections that soften the rule either require information that most European providers do not supply or turn every year's increase in value into ordinary income. For US persons, including those living abroad, US-domiciled funds are therefore the normal choice.

## Fund size and age (step 3)

Below a fund size of about $50 million to $100 million, running an ETF hardly pays for itself. From around $100 million, the industry regards a product as cost-efficient and at low risk of closure. Age is the second filter criterion. For a fund with a twelve-month history, no reliable tracking difference can be determined; that requires at least three to five years.

A large fund size, on the other hand, does not guarantee narrow spreads. The [[Bid-ask spread|bid-ask spread]] depends on the liquidity of the stocks held and on the market makers, not on the size of the fund. For the large broad US ETFs, it is often one or two cents on a share price of several hundred dollars during regular trading hours from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time. In the first and last minutes of the session and in pre-market and after-hours trading, spreads are considerably wider. For funds with foreign stocks, the underlying markets are partly closed during US trading hours, so prices are based on estimates.

bloecke.titel: Types of cost for a small and a large portfolio
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation in dollars a year with a monthly contribution of $300 ($3,600 a year). The first series shows the first year with an average portfolio value of $1,950, built up linearly with no return assumed; the second shows the same plan at a portfolio value of $100,000. The large online brokers charge no commission on US-listed ETFs; a half spread of one basis point is assumed on each of the twelve purchases.

bloecke.md: Since the large online brokers dropped commissions on US-listed stocks and ETFs in 2019, the broker hardly determines the cost of investing small amounts anymore. Fractional shares let you invest exactly $300 instead of buying whole shares. That leaves the expense ratio as the cost that grows with the portfolio. A difference of 0.17 percentage points amounts to $170 a year on $100,000, permanently and without any action by the investor. Commission-free trading is financed in part by payment for order flow from market makers. In the US, this is permitted and disclosed in each broker's quarterly report under SEC Rule 606.

- An ETF can be closed. According to industry counts, around 230 ETFs were liquidated in the US in 2025. Signs of this are a small fund size, low trading volume and many competing products on the same index.
- For niche and thematic products, there are figures from Morningstar (observation period ending mid-2024). Of the thematic funds, 94% survived the first year; after ten years, three in four were still in existence, and after fifteen years, 45%.
- The index can change. In 2012 and 2013, for example, Vanguard moved a number of its index funds from MSCI benchmarks to CRSP and FTSE indices, citing lower licensing costs. The ticker and name can stay the same while the content changes.
- In a merger, the fund is absorbed into another fund. Such reorganizations are usually structured to be tax-free; the details are in the proxy or information statement sent to shareholders.

A holding in a taxable account is worth $20,000, of which $8,000 is unrealized long-term gain. If the fund is liquidated, it is settled at net asset value. This amounts to a sale that the investor did not choose.

At a rate of 15%, the tax is $1,200, money that would otherwise have stayed invested. Over a further fifteen years at 6%, the portfolio is around $2,880 smaller at the end. Without the liquidation, the tax on the gain to date would be due on a sale after these fifteen years, so the disadvantage after tax is around $1,420 (illustrative calculation). If the shares had been held until death, the gain would never have been taxed, because heirs receive a cost basis stepped up to the market value (26 U.S.C. § 1014). The disadvantage arises from the forced timing of taxation rather than from the fund itself. This is why fund size is also a tax criterion for selection. In an IRA or 401(k), a liquidation costs no tax.

schritte.text: First, decide whether the US market alone, the whole world or the whole world including small caps should be covered. The decision is made before any product search and is recorded in writing.
Exact index name, fund size above $100 million, launched at least three years ago, registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940 and domiciled in the US.
Set the values for three to five years side by side instead of sorting by expense ratio. Without a history, no judgement is possible.

Legal structure (1940 Act fund, trust, partnership or ETN), extent of securities lending according to the annual report, history of capital gain distributions and, for international funds, the pass-through of foreign taxes.
Clarify whether the ETF can be bought there without commission and in fractional shares, whether automatic investing is available for it and in which account (taxable, IRA, 401(k)) it will be held.
Buy with a limit order during regular trading hours and then check the fact sheet once a year. In a taxable account, switching without a reason costs tax on the gain to date.

bloecke.titel: Where to find the fund information
bloecke.md:
- The summary prospectus at the front of the prospectus states the expense ratio, the investment objective, the principal risks and the past performance.
- The full prospectus and the statement of additional information (SAI) describe the legal structure, the tax treatment and securities lending.
- The annual and semi-annual shareholder reports show the actual costs, the distributions and the income from securities lending.
- The provider's website lists the holdings, usually daily, and the distribution history.
- All filings are available free of charge in the SEC's EDGAR database. Comparison sites are suitable for tracking difference and fund size; always read the reference date and the scope of the figures as well.

The index determines the return, the fund structure determines how it is taxed, and the expense ratio accounts for hundredths to tenths of a percentage point. If you check these three levels in this order and stay with US-domiciled funds, you will arrive at a sound result with any of the large broad ETFs, even though none of them is perfect.

mitnehmen: The choice of index (US only or the whole world, with or without small caps) determines the return; all further decisions shift it only by fractions.
For comparison purposes, what counts is the tracking difference over several years rather than the expense ratio alone; broad core ETFs typically charge 0.03% to 0.10% a year.
Fund size and age are criteria for a fund's survival, because below about $100 million the risk of closure rises, and in a taxable account a liquidation forces a taxable sale.

The legal structure determines the tax: 1940 Act ETFs pass through the normal rates, gold trusts are taxed as collectibles at up to 28%, and foreign funds such as UCITS ETFs are PFICs that US persons should avoid.
With commission-free trading and fractional shares, the expense ratio is the main ongoing cost; a difference of 0.17 percentage points costs $170 a year on $100,000.

begriffe.text: Country in which a fund is established. For US persons, funds domiciled outside the US are generally passive foreign investment companies (PFICs) with punitive taxation, so US-domiciled funds are the normal choice.

One of several tranches of the same fund with its own ticker but shared fund assets. At Vanguard, for example, many ETFs are a share class of an index mutual fund. This explains why portals give very different sizes for the same product.
Unsecured debt security of a bank whose payout tracks an index. It is traded like an ETF but holds no assets of its own, and the buyer bears the issuer's default risk.

Closure of a fund by its sponsor. Shareholders receive the net asset value in cash; in a taxable account, the gain accumulated up to that point is realized and taxed, regardless of whether the timing suits the investor.

US law regulating mutual funds and most ETFs. Registered funds must hold their assets with a custodian, have a board with independent directors and publish a prospectus and regular shareholder reports.
